content.overview: Section 2 is the definitional gateway for the Companies Act, 2013. Unless the context otherwise requires, the terms defined in section 2 control the meaning of those terms throughout the Act. Load-bearing clauses for exam and practice include company (s. 2(20)), private company (s. 2(68)), public company (s. 2(71)), One Person Company (s. 2(62)), holding company (s. 2(46)), subsidiary company or subsidiary (s. 2(87)), small company (s. 2(85)), key managerial personnel (s. 2(51)), officer who is in default (s. 2(60)), related party (s. 2(76)), and deposit (s. 2(31)). Numeric thresholds in some definitions (notably small company) have been amended by later notifications and Amendment Acts; the threshold in force on the relevant date must be checked.
content.glance: Identify the exact clause of s. 2; apply the statutory words including provisos and explanations; check later amendments to thresholds; do not treat a foreign-incorporated body as a ‘company’ under s. 2(20) merely because it does business in India.
content.study:
Section 2 defines persons, securities, offices and relationships used throughout the Act.

Method
1. Identify the exact clause (e.g. s. 2(68), not a textbook label).
2. Apply the statutory text, including provisos and explanations.
3. Check whether the context otherwise requires a different meaning.
4. For threshold-based definitions (especially small company), verify the figures in force on the relevant date.

Selected load-bearing definitions (official text summary)
• Company — s. 2(20): a company incorporated under this Act or under any previous company law.
• Private company — s. 2(68): a company having a minimum paid-up share capital as may be prescribed, and which by its articles (i) restricts the right to transfer its shares; (ii) except in the case of a One Person Company, limits the number of its members to two hundred (joint holders treated as a single member; employees and certain former employees not counted); and (iii) prohibits any invitation to the public to subscribe for any securities of the company.
• Public company — s. 2(71): a company which is not a private company and has a minimum paid-up share capital as may be prescribed. A company which is a subsidiary of a company not being a private company is deemed to be a public company for the purposes of the Act even if it continues to be a private company in its articles.
• One Person Company — s. 2(62): a company which has only one person as a member.
• Holding company — s. 2(46): in relation to one or more other companies, a company of which such companies are subsidiary companies.
• Subsidiary company or subsidiary — s. 2(87): in relation to any other company (the holding company), a company in which the holding company controls the composition of the Board of Directors, or exercises or controls more than one-half of the total voting power either at its own or together with one or more of its subsidiary companies. Explanations address layers of subsidiaries and other control concepts as in the Act.
• Small company — s. 2(85): a company other than a public company whose paid-up share capital and turnover do not exceed such amounts as may be prescribed (thresholds have been raised by notification; always verify the figures in force for the relevant year).
• Key managerial personnel — s. 2(51): includes CEO or managing director or manager; company secretary; whole-time director; CFO; and such other officer as may be prescribed / designated by the Board within the statutory limits.
• Officer who is in default — s. 2(60): whole-time director; KMP; where no KMP is appointed, such director or directors as specified by the Board or all directors; and other persons charged with responsibility as listed in the clause.
• Related party — s. 2(76): director or his relative; KMP or his relative; firm in which a director, manager or relative is a partner; private company in which a director or manager or relative is a member or director; public company in which a director or manager is a director or holds specified shareholding; body corporate whose board, managing director or manager is accustomed to act in accordance with the advice of a director or manager; and other persons as prescribed.
• Deposit — s. 2(31): any receipt of money by way of deposit or loan or in any other form by a company, subject to the exclusions prescribed in the definition and the Deposit Rules.

Boundary
Section 2 is definitional. Substantive duties and consequences sit in the operative sections that use these terms. Foreign companies are dealt with in Chapter XXII and are not ‘companies’ under s. 2(20) merely by carrying on business in India.

sections.heading: Company — s. 2(20)
sections.body: Company means a company incorporated under this Act or under any previous company law.

sections.heading: Private company — s. 2(68)
sections.body: Articles must restrict transfer of shares, limit members to two hundred (except OPC; joint holders as one; employees carve-out), and prohibit public invitation for securities. Minimum paid-up capital as may be prescribed.

sections.heading: Public company — s. 2(71)
sections.body: Not a private company; minimum paid-up capital as may be prescribed. Subsidiary of a non-private company is deemed public even if its articles still describe it as private.

sections.heading: OPC, holding and subsidiary
sections.body: OPC (s. 2(62)): only one member. Holding (s. 2(46)): company of which others are subsidiaries. Subsidiary (s. 2(87)): Board-composition control or more than one-half of total voting power, including through subsidiaries, as provided in the clause and explanations.

sections.heading: Small company, KMP, officer in default, related party, deposit
sections.body: Small company (s. 2(85)): non-public company within prescribed capital and turnover limits (check current notification). KMP (s. 2(51)), officer who is in default (s. 2(60)), related party (s. 2(76)) and deposit (s. 2(31)) as defined in those clauses and connected rules.

examples.title: Private company test
examples.body: Articles restrict transfer, limit members to 200 (non-OPC) and prohibit public invitation for securities. Subject to prescribed capital, the company is a private company under s. 2(68).

examples.title: Deemed public company
examples.body: A private company is a subsidiary of a public company. Under the proviso to s. 2(71) it is deemed a public company for the purposes of the Act even if its articles still call it private.

examples.title: Subsidiary by voting power
examples.body: Holding company controls more than one-half of the total voting power in another company. That other company is a subsidiary under s. 2(87), subject to the statutory explanations.

hypotheticals.question: Which clause decides whether a company is private?
hypotheticals.analysis: Section 2(68), read with the articles and the statutory carve-outs (including the OPC exception and the joint-holder and employee rules). Do not use the Companies Act, 1956 member limit.

hypotheticals.question: Is every entity that does business in India a ‘company’ under s. 2(20)?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Section 2(20) requires incorporation under this Act or a previous company law. Foreign companies are addressed under Chapter XXII.

distinctions.title: Private company (s. 2(68)) vs public company (s. 2(71))
distinctions.left: Articles restrict transfer, limit members, prohibit public invitation
distinctions.right: Not private; subsidiary of non-private is deemed public

rows.left: Closed membership and no public offer

misconceptions.trap: A company is private merely because it has few members.
misconceptions.correction: Section 2(68) requires the three article conditions (transfer restriction, member limit, no public invitation), not mere small size.
Section 2(85) uses prescribed capital and turnover limits that have been amended by notification; always check the figures in force for the relevant period.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a Section 2 problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Identify the term and the exact clause of s. 2. II. Apply the statutory text including provisos and explanations. III. Check context and any later threshold amendment. IV. Conclude for the operative section that uses the term.

bareActPointers: Connected rules and notifications for prescribed amounts
examTips: Cite the clause number, not only the label.
For private vs public, state the three article conditions and the deeming proviso.
For small company, flag that thresholds are prescribed and may have changed.
revisionPoints: KMP, officer in default, related party, deposit
